assumptions: USD and physical units. Toy homogeneous production batch, normal spoilage absorbed into good units, abnormal spoilage separately expensed at pre-spoilage cost less its salvage. No opening inventory, no other scrap recovery.

evidence.text: [Production] 10,000 input units at $40 each including all conversion cost; 500 spoiled units, 9,500 good units. Normal spoilage allowance 2% of input units.

[Policy] Abnormal spoilage is measured at $40/unit and removed from production cost pool. Scrap salvage of $600 relates only to abnormal spoiled units and offsets the separate loss. Normal spoilage has no salvage.
[Inventory] All 9,500 good units completed and held at reporting date, no sales or NRV issue.
[Draft] Controller proposes allocating all $400,000 production cost to 9,500 good units, with salvage posted as miscellaneous income.
[Quality] Engineering investigation into excess spoilage is still pending; no evidence identifies a specific cause.

qas.question: Find normal spoilage units allowed at the stated standard.
Find abnormal spoilage units for the current production batch.
Find total cost assigned to abnormal spoilage, net of salvage.
Find total cost remaining for good units and normal spoilage.
Calculate current good-unit cost under normal spoilage absorption.
Explain why salvage from abnormal spoiled units does not reduce ordinary good-unit carrying cost here.
qas.answer: The toy assigns salvage to the abnormal-spoilage loss, reducing its separate expense, not the normal production cost pool.

qas.question: Why does the controller's proposal to absorb all spoilage over good units misstate inventory?
qas.answer: It capitalizes abnormal spoilage rather than expensing its net loss immediately; only normal spoilage is absorbed under the policy.

qas.question: Can responsibility for the abnormal spoilage be attributed to a specific machine operator?
qas.answer: No. The records show excess spoiled units, not the causal equipment or operator investigation.

assumptions: USD million. Toy sales with right of return: estimate refund liability on expected refunds, recovery asset at original inventory cost less recovery handling costs. Actual refunds and returned inventory settle respective balances. No tax.

evidence.text: [Sales] Gross cash sales 200m; expected refund 8% of gross sales. Goods sold had original cost 120m. Expected returns have the same cost-to-price ratio; expected recovery handling costs 1m.

[Returns] During same year, 6m cash refunds paid and returned goods with original cost 3.6m physically recovered; no recovery handling cost paid yet. Estimate of total expected refunds 16m remains inclusive of those settled.

[Policy] Refund liability = total expected refunds less paid. Recovery asset initially = expected original cost of returns less 1m expected handling cost, reduced by 3.6m goods recovered; no additional estimate change.
[Other] Selling/admin expense 30m cash. No opening balances.
[Memo] Controller records all 200m as revenue and waits until each return is received to recognize refunds.

qas.question: Find initially recognized sales revenue net of expected refunds.
Find initial recovery asset from expected returns.
Find cost of sales after initial recovery asset recognition.
Find remaining refund liability at reporting date.
Find remaining recovery asset after recovered goods move back to inventory.
Why do the paid refunds of 6m not create another reduction of net revenue?
qas.answer: They settle part of the already recognized expected refund liability; no estimate change occurred.

qas.question: Can refund liability be offset against the recovery asset?
qas.answer: No under the specified separate presentation; one is a cash refund obligation, the other a recovery right to goods.

qas.question: Can actual future return percentage be known exactly from the estimate?
qas.answer: No. Expected refunds are an estimate; future customer decisions and actual returns are uncertain.

assumptions: USD million. Toy modified loan retains recognition; recalculate gross carrying amount using discounted modified contractual flows at original EIR. Modification loss separate from ECL. No tax.

evidence.text: [Loan] Gross carrying amount immediately before modification 100m, original EIR 10%, existing allowance 5m. No accrued unpaid coupon outside carrying amount.
[Modified contract] Borrower pays 35m at end year1 and 80m at end year2. No immediate fee, principal or cash settlement at modification date.
[Assessment] Modification does not qualify for derecognition. Toy new gross carrying =35/1.10+80/1.10²; updated ECL at modification 9m independent of modification loss.
[P&L] Operating profit before modification and incremental ECL 20m. No other impairment or finance item.
[Draft] Credit manager uses nominal modified cash 115m as new carrying, books 15m gain.

qas.question: Find PV of the first modified contractual payment.
Find modified gross carrying under original EIR.
Calculate modification gain/loss at the modification date.
Find incremental ECL charge from updated allowance.
Find net carrying after modification and new allowance.
Why is 115m nominal total not the carrying amount at modification?
qas.answer: Payments occur in future periods; the stipulated model discounts at the original EIR.

qas.question: Should the modification loss automatically replace the ECL charge?
qas.answer: No. Modification adjusts contractual cash-flow PV; ECL measures separate expected credit loss.

qas.question: Can subsequent default probability be calculated from the modified payments?
qas.answer: No. Contractual cash flows do not disclose probability or recovery distribution.

assumptions: USD million. Simplified fictional insurance group test: remaining expected cash outflows plus risk adjustment less future premium inflows gives onerous deficit; recognized loss component released by improvement, capped at existing balance. No discount changes.

evidence.text: [Initial group] Future premiums 120m, expected claims/expenses 130m, risk adjustment 8m. No opening loss component. Toy initial onerous loss equals excess outflows plus adjustment over premiums.
[Revision] Before service begins, revised claims/expenses fall to 115m, premiums remain 120m, risk adjustment becomes 7m.
[Policy] Reverse previous loss only to extent deficit reduces; no gain beyond original loss. No cash flows or service revenue have occurred.
[Company P&L] Other groups generate profit 35m before initial loss and subsequent reversal in same period.
[Memo] Actuary's dashboard labels the 15m reduction in expected claims as an immediate cash saving.

qas.question: Find initial onerous deficit.
Find revised deficit before service.
Find loss component reversal following revised estimate.
Find remaining loss component after revision.
Find company profit after both initial charge and reversal.
Why is the 16m reversal different from the 15m claims estimate reduction?
qas.answer: The risk adjustment also falls by 1m; both affect the deficit.

qas.question: Does the estimate reduction establish actual current cash saving?
qas.answer: No. No service or cash settlement has occurred.

qas.question: Can a real IFRS 17 contractual service margin be derived from this toy?
qas.answer: No. The full measurement model and contract data are not supplied.

assumptions: USD million. Toy qualifying development expenditure starts only after documented feasibility gate; prior research expensed. Amortize completed asset from ready-for-use date, straight-line, zero residual. No tax.

evidence.text: [Timeline] Jan–Mar research 9m before feasibility approval Apr 1. Apr–Sep qualifying development 18m. Oct–Dec post-launch maintenance 6m, not qualifying. All cash paid.
[Asset] Software ready for use Oct 1; useful life 3 years. No opening development asset and no impairment.
[P&L] Revenue 60m from all products, other operating expense 30m before research/development/maintenance/amortization.
[Cash] CFO before project expenditure 30m. Toy research and maintenance CFO; capitalized development CFI.
[Draft] CTO capitalizes all 33m spending because the product ultimately launched.

qas.question: Find qualifying capitalized development addition.
Find current year amortization from Oct 1.
Find closing development asset carrying amount.
Find operating profit after all properly classified expenses.
Find CFO after noncapitalized project cash costs.
Why does eventual project success not retroactively capitalize research costs?
qas.answer: The stipulated eligibility begins at the documented gate; earlier research remains expensed.

qas.question: Why is post-launch maintenance excluded from development asset?
qas.answer: It maintains existing functionality and is expressly nonqualifying under the toy.

qas.question: Can product-specific ROI be calculated from total company revenue 60?
qas.answer: No. Incremental product cash flows and attributable cost are missing.

assumptions: USD million. Toy single plant asset has no goodwill. Impairment reversal limited to carrying amount that would exist absent prior impairment. Depreciation straight-line; no tax.

evidence.text: [Historical] Plant acquired for 100m with 10-year life, zero residual. End of year4 pre-impairment carrying 60m; impairment 24m reduces it to 36m. Remaining life six years.
[Year5] Depreciate impaired carrying over six years. At year5 end updated recoverable amount 70m due to approved tariff recovery; no additions/disposals.
[Policy] Reverse impairment only to lower of recoverable amount and hypothetical carrying absent prior impairment. No goodwill.
[P&L] Year5 operating profit before depreciation and reversal 20m. No other income.
[Memo] Management proposes raising carrying directly to 70m.

qas.question: Find year5 depreciation on the impaired carrying value.
Find carrying immediately before year5 reversal test.
Find hypothetical carrying absent original impairment at year5 end.
Find permitted reversal under the specified cap.
Find year5 operating profit including depreciation and permitted reversal.
Why may the 70m recoverable amount not become carrying value under this model?
qas.answer: The reversal is capped at 50m, the no-impairment hypothetical carrying amount.

qas.question: Does the reversal imply 20m of cash proceeds were received?
qas.answer: No. It is a noncash carrying-value adjustment.

qas.question: Can the tariff-related recoverable amount be independently verified?
qas.answer: No. Future cash flow forecast and discount inputs are not supplied.

assumptions: USD million. Toy property fair-value gain recognized P&L; tax base historical, tax rate 25%, deferred tax recognized. Disposal next year settles tax on realized gain and releases DTL. No other tax differences.

evidence.text: [Opening] Property carrying and tax base both 200m. Year1 fair value increases to 260m. No depreciation under the toy; tax basis unchanged.
[Year1] Other pretax earnings 30m fully taxable; FV gain excluded from current taxable income. Current tax paid in full.
[Year2 disposal] Property sold for 270m, no selling costs. Taxable realized gain based on 200m tax base. No other income or expense. Current tax paid in full.
[Policy] Year1 DTL on FV gain, year2 release when asset sold. Tax rate 25% both years.
[Draft] CFO books year2 total tax expense equal to 17.5m current tax without releasing DTL.

qas.question: Find year1 fair-value gain recognized in profit.
Find year1 closing deferred tax liability.
Find year1 total tax expense including current and deferred components.
Find year2 accounting disposal gain before tax.
Find year2 total tax expense after DTL release.
Explain why year2 cash tax exceeds year2 tax expense.
qas.answer: Cash tax 17.5 includes previously deferred year1 taxable gain; releasing DTL 15 leaves 2.5 current-period total expense.

qas.question: Should the year1 DTL remain after the property is fully disposed of?
qas.answer: No. The temporary difference is realized and the liability is released.

qas.question: Can the property's real tax treatment under a specific jurisdiction be inferred?
qas.answer: No. The tax basis and rate here are stipulated fictional rules.

assumptions: USD million. Fictional private investment valuation uses enterprise value = normalized EBITDA × multiple, minus net debt, times ownership share, then specified liquidity discount. No other assets/liabilities in holding.

evidence.text: [Operating] Portfolio company reported EBITDA 24m includes one-time settlement gain 4m; valuation policy excludes it. Net debt 50m.
[Valuation] Approved market multiple 8x on normalized EBITDA. Fund holds 30% of equity; liquidity discount 10% applies to stake value after debt and ownership.
[NAV] Opening carrying of stake 27m; rest of fund NAV unchanged at 100m. No transactions, distributions or fees.
[Sensitivity] Multiple scenarios 7x and 9x with EBITDA/debt/discount unchanged. No probability weighting.
[Memo] Investment team applies multiple directly to reported EBITDA and deducts debt only after multiplying by 30%.

qas.question: Find normalized EBITDA used in approved valuation.
Find portfolio company equity value before minority stake discount.
Find fair value of the fund's stake after liquidity discount.
Find NAV after replacing old carrying value.
Find stake valuation at the lower 7x multiple.
Explain why subtracting the company's full net debt after applying 30% is wrong.
qas.answer: Debt is a claim on the whole enterprise; compute total equity value first, then the stake share and discount.

qas.question: Does approved valuation of 29.7 establish executable exit proceeds?
qas.answer: No. The valuation is model-based and not a binding offer.

qas.question: Can a probability-weighted fair value be calculated from the 7x and 9x sensitivities?
qas.answer: No. Scenario probabilities are not supplied.
